Regulation

# NMC public notice March 2026: what it means for students

Notification U-15024/15/2024-UGMEB(Pt), dated 5 March 2026, signed by Ram Pratap, Director UGMEB. Five clarifications that decide whether a foreign degree converts into an Indian registration. The official PDF is below, and everything here is checked against it.

Reviewed 22 November 2026. Always read the regulator's copy before you act on a summary, including this one.

## On this page

1. The official PDF

2. The five clarifications

3. Every official document

4. Timeline, 2002 to 2026

5. FMGL 2021, seven rules

6. Philippines compliance checklist

7. FMGE against NExT

8. FMGE eligibility

9. Documents to keep forever

10. Questions

## Download the notice

Verify the document, not the screenshot

This is the authentic NMC Public Notice U-15024/15/2024-UGMEB(Pt), dated 5 March 2026, signed by Ram Pratap, Director UGMEB, and digitally signed by Dr. Raghav Langer, Secretary NMC, on 6 March 2026. Six pages, five clarifications. WhatsApp forwards of a single page are how people end up acting on a rule that does not exist.

### NMC Public Notice, March 2026

Mandatory physical onsite compensation. Six pages. Notification U-15024/15/2024-UGMEB(Pt).

[Download PDF](https://drdreams.in/NMC-Public-Notice-March-2026.pdf)
        
        
          How to use it

Show it to your university registrar when you ask for a compensation certificate, and check that the certificate carries the extended period, the subjects and the clerkship detail that the notice requires. State Medical Councils verify against this exact document, so keep a digital copy and a printed one.

## The five clarifications

Read these in order. The first one decides which rulebook applies to you, and you do not get to choose.

### 1. Which rulebook applies, decided by your admission date

If you joined your foreign course **before 18 November 2021**, you are governed by the Screening Test Regulations 2002, provided you compensated your online study with physical onsite clinical or theory training, completed a year of internship at the foreign university, and passed examinations equivalent to the Indian MBBS.

If you joined **on or after 18 November 2021**, the FMGL Regulations 2021 and the CRMI Regulations 2021 apply. That means a one-year compulsory rotating internship in India after your foreign degree. The conditions in the 7 December 2023 notice remain in force.

"The students who had taken admission on or before 18.11.2021, the date of notification of the Foreign Medical Graduate Licentiate Regulations, 2021, and who have duly compensated the period of online instruction by undergoing physical onsite clinical and/or theory training, together with one year of internship in the concerned foreign medical college or university, and who have qualified the examinations equivalent to the MBBS examination in India, shall be considered in accordance with the provisions of the Screening Test Regulations."

Source: NMC Public Notice U-15024/15/2024-UGMEB(Pt), 5 March 2026

### 2. Online study cannot be compensated without extending the course

This is the sentence that invalidates a lot of certificates already sitting in students' files. Compensation without an extension of the study period is not accepted. The course and clerkship must be comparable with the Indian MBBS under the Graduate Medical Education Regulations 1997, and medical training needs substantial hands-on clinical work that virtual instruction cannot replace.

If any part of your course was online, you need equivalent in-person training for that exact duration.

"Compensation without extension of the study period is not acceptable, as it is contrary to FMGL Regulations, 2021, which require the course and clerkship to be commensurate with the MBBS course in India... foreign medical institutions that issue a 'compensation certificate' without actually extending the period of study and without ensuring that the additional training has occurred in a physical mode are acting in contradiction to the intent and requirements of the FMGL Regulations. Such certificates, issued without genuine compensation and extension of study period, undermine the very spirit and purpose of the FMGL Regulations, 2021."

Source: NMC Public Notice U-15024/15/2024-UGMEB(Pt), 5 March 2026

### 3. What a valid compensation certificate must contain

The certificate has to specify the subjects completed during offline compensation, both theory and practical; the clinical subjects undertaken onsite; the mandatory clerkship completed during the compensation period; and the extended academic period, meaning the exact duration added. The transcript of record must also be apostilled and authenticated by the Indian embassy or high commission in that country.

"It is imperative to verify the authenticity of the claim of Foreign Medical Graduates (FMGs) regarding the offline compensation for the remaining duration of the medical course, which must include both theoretical and practical components. Accordingly, the compensation certificate issued by the concerned foreign medical institution must clearly specify the details of the subjects and the duration completed by the FMG, i.e., The certificate must specify theory, clinical subjects, and mandatory clerkship undertaken during offline compensation, etc."

Source: NMC Public Notice U-15024/15/2024-UGMEB(Pt), 5 March 2026

### 4. Two academic years cannot be compressed into one

The notice answers this directly, because students were trying it. Academic years cannot be compressed, and the whole online period must be compensated with physical onsite training. You cannot finish a two-year curriculum in one year of offline study.

"Whether the curriculum for the two academic years can be completed in one year of offline study? No. As clarified at Sl. No. 1, academic years cannot be compressed, and the entire online study period must be adequately compensated through physical onsite training."

Source: NMC Public Notice U-15024/15/2024-UGMEB(Pt), 5 March 2026

### 5. State Medical Councils carry the verification

Primary responsibility for processing foreign medical graduate applications sits with the State Medical Councils, in consultation with the State Directorates of Medical Education. They must confirm that the compensatory academics happened at the same foreign institution, verify visa stamps and entry and exit records, confirm the screening test, and confirm the one-year CRMI in India.

The sequence is: qualify the screening test and submit the degree and clerkship certificates, get provisional registration for CRMI, then get permanent registration after completing it. No council may grant permanent registration without full verification, and a registration granted outside these rules can be revoked.

"The primary responsibility for processing applications of Foreign Medical Graduates (FMGs)... rests exclusively with the respective State Medical Councils (SMCs), in consultation with the concerned State Directorate of Medical Education (DME)."

Source: NMC Public Notice U-15024/15/2024-UGMEB(Pt), 5 March 2026
        

        
          If you studied in the Philippines between 2020 and 2022

Contact your university now and ask for a compensation certificate that states the extended period. Get the transcript apostilled and authenticated at the Indian embassy in Manila. Do not wait until graduation, when the registrar has less reason to help you and you have less time to fix it.

## Every official document in one place

Links go to the regulator or to the stored copy. Read the source, not a summary of the source.

### NMC Screening Test Regulations, 2002

The foundation law, with amendments up to 2018 that made NEET mandatory for admission abroad.

[Open PDF](https://www.nmc.org.in/wp-content/uploads/2017/10/Screen-Test-Regulations-1.pdf)

### NMC e-Gazette, all FMGL and CRMI notifications

FMGL Regulations 2021, CRMI Regulations 2021, and every amendment since.

[Visit NMC](https://www.nmc.org.in/e-gazette/e-gazette-nmc/)

### FMGE June 2026 information bulletin

Exam rules, eligibility, documents and attempt limits, published by NBEMS.

[Open bulletin](https://nbe.edu.in/IB/FMGE%20JUNE%202026%20information%20bulletin.pdf)

### NMC guidelines for registration of foreign medical graduates, 2022

Which students fall under the 2002 rules and which under the 2021 FMGL rules.

[Open PDF](https://www.nmc.org.in/MCIRest/open/getDocument?path=/Documents/Public/Portal/LatestNews/Document%20(1).pdf)

### NMC public notice, 19 June 2024

Clarifies that students who compensated online classes with onsite training are eligible for the one-year CRMI.

[Visit NMC](https://www.nmc.org.in/e-gazette/e-gazette-nmc/)

### NMC public notice, 7 December 2023

Ukraine relaxations, BS course recognition, the 7.5 per cent internship cap, the 10-year limit and eligibility certificates.

[Visit NMC](https://www.nmc.org.in/e-gazette/e-gazette-nmc/)

## Timeline, 2002 to 2026

Every rule that changes what your degree is worth in India, in the order it happened.

-

### 2002: Screening Test Regulations

MCI introduces FMGE. Every foreign medical graduate must pass it to practise in India. No NEET requirement yet.

-

### 2018: NEET becomes mandatory for studying abroad

An amendment makes NEET compulsory for Indian students seeking admission to a foreign medical college.

-

### 18 November 2021: FMGL Regulations

NMC replaces MCI. A 54-month minimum course, a 12-month internship at the same foreign university, WDOMS listing, NEET and English medium instruction all become conditions.

-

### 18 November 2021: CRMI Regulations

Compulsory rotating internship in India for every post-2021 foreign graduate, with a 7.5 per cent seat cap in older colleges.

-

### 7 December 2023: public notice

Ukraine relaxations, recognition of the BS course for pre-2021 students, the 7.5 per cent cap, the 10-year limit, and eligibility certificate rules.

-

### 19 June 2024: public notice

Students who genuinely compensated online teaching with onsite training remain eligible for CRMI.

-

### 8 May 2025: CHED letter

The Philippine Commission on Higher Education tells the Indian Embassy that the Doctor of Medicine meets the FMGL conditions: 54 months, the prescribed subjects, English, a twelve month internship, and a certificate of registrability.

### 5 March 2026: NMC public notice

Compensation must extend the course, certificates without an extension are invalid, academic years cannot be compressed, and State Medical Councils carry verification. The PDF is at the top of this page.

### 11 March 2026: House Resolution No. 73

The House of Representatives of the Philippines endorses that the MD from CHED-recognised institutions complies with the NMC regulations for Indian students abroad.

### 17 June 2026: Embassy advisory

The Embassy of India, Manila sets out the position in writing, with the CHED letter and the Resolution. [The PLE page](https://drdreams.in/ple-philippines.md) has the sequence.

### November 2026: the PLE opens

The Philippine Professional Regulation Commission tells the Embassy that Indian graduates of recognised Philippine medical schools can sit the Physician Licensure Examination and register to practise. [What that means](https://drdreams.in/ple-philippines.md).

## FMGL 2021: seven rules that cannot be worked around

Break any one of these and the degree does not convert into an Indian registration. The 2026 notice adds detail to them, it does not relax them.

1.

### 54 months of academic study

At least four and a half years, excluding internship, comparable with the Indian MBBS curriculum. Older four-year programmes no longer qualify.

2.

### 12-month internship at the same institution

Not at another hospital, and not in India. Same university as the academic course.

3.

### NEET before admission

Qualify NEET-UG before joining the foreign medical degree. BSBio sits before the degree, which is why it is treated differently.

4.

### English medium

The whole course in English, with an English medium certificate from the university.

5.

### WDOMS listing

The university must appear in the World Directory of Medical Schools. Check [search.wdoms.org](https://search.wdoms.org) before paying anything.

6.

### Same institution for study and internship

Transfers between universities are generally not permitted, outside specific NMC-approved schemes.

7.

### Eligibility certificate

Students joining after 2021 should obtain an NMC eligibility certificate before joining the course.

## The Philippines checklist

No ban

There is no ban on studying medicine in the Philippines in 2026. There is tighter verification. The degree works if the college is listed, the course meets 54 months, and the internship was onsite at the same institution.

### Before admission

- College listed on WDOMS

- 54-month programme, confirmed in writing

- NEET qualified before MD

- NMC eligibility certificate

- English medium certificate available

### During study

- Passport with valid visa stamps and entry and exit records

- If any online study, a certificate stating the extended period

- Transcript naming theory, clinical subjects and clerkship

- 12-month internship at the same university

### After graduation

- Transcript apostilled and authenticated in Manila

- FMGE cleared

- Provisional registration with the state council

- 12-month CRMI in India

- Permanent registration after verification

Two promises that are always false

An "internship in India to save cost", offered instead of the foreign internship, is something the regulations do not allow. A "compensation certificate" issued without an extension of your course is the certificate this notice invalidates.

## FMGE against NExT

As of this review, FMGE remains the active screening test. NExT has been deferred more than once, so prepare for the syllabus rather than the name of the exam.

| Feature | FMGE | NExT (proposed) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Status** | Active | Deferred |
| **Who sits it** | Foreign medical graduates only | All graduates, Indian and foreign |
| **Frequency** | Twice a year | Twice a year, proposed |
| **Pass mark** | 50 per cent | To be notified |
| **Attempts** | Unlimited | Limited, proposed |
| **Syllabus** | Close to the full MBBS curriculum in both cases |  |

Where the two exams stand, and how they differ.

Verify the current position on [nmc.org.in](https://www.nmc.org.in) and with NBEMS before you plan around either exam.

## FMGE eligibility, in five conditions

1.

### A primary medical qualification from outside India

An MD or MBBS equivalent awarded by a foreign institution.

2.

### WDOMS listing at the time of admission

Not later, and not "in process".

3.

### NEET qualified before joining

For admissions after 2018.

4.

### 54 months of study and 12 months of internship

Both at the same institution, with the internship onsite.

5.

### Valid compensation, if any study was online

With the extended period stated, as the March 2026 notice requires.

## Documents to keep for the rest of your career

Lose any of these and the paperwork becomes a project. Keep originals, scans and a cloud copy.

### Academic

- 12th marksheet and pass certificate

- NEET scorecard and admit card

- BSBio transcript, if you took that route

- MD degree certificate

- Full academic transcript

- English medium certificate

### Clinical and internship

- Internship completion certificate

- Compensation certificate, if any study was online

- Clinical logbook

- Clerkship completion proof

### Verification

- Passport with every visa stamp and entry and exit record

- Apostilled degree and transcript

- Indian embassy authentication

- NMC eligibility certificate

### Exam and registration

- FMGE pass certificate

- Provisional registration

- CRMI completion certificate

- Permanent registration

Questions

## What people ask about these rules

What is the new NMC notification of March 2026 about?

It clarifies that online study cannot be compensated without genuinely extending the study period, sets out what a valid compensation certificate must contain, confirms that academic years cannot be compressed, and places verification responsibility on State Medical Councils.

Where can I download the March 2026 notification?

The official PDF of notification U-15024/15/2024-UGMEB(Pt) is linked at the top of this page. Always use the regulator's copy rather than a screenshot or a forwarded image.

Is there a ban on Philippines MBBS in 2026?

There is no ban. There is tighter verification. The degree is treated as valid only if the college is listed with NMC and WDOMS, the course meets the 54-month requirement, and the internship was completed onsite at the same institution.

[The six colleges covered here](https://drdreams.in/colleges.md) are checked against both lists. Verify them yourself anyway.

What is the 54-month rule?

Under the FMGL Regulations 2021 the foreign medical course must run at least 54 months of academic study, excluding internship, and must be comparable with the Indian MBBS curriculum. Older four-year programmes no longer qualify.

What must a compensation certificate contain?

The subjects completed during offline compensation, both theory and practical. The clinical subjects undertaken onsite. The mandatory clerkship. And the extended academic period, meaning the exact duration added. Certificates without a genuine extension are invalid.

I joined before 18 November 2021. Which rules apply?

The Screening Test Regulations 2002, provided you compensated online study with physical onsite training and completed a year of internship at the foreign university. Students who joined later fall under FMGL 2021 and CRMI 2021, including the one-year internship in India.

Is the Philippines MD valid in India in 2026?

Yes, if the college is NMC-listed and WDOMS-listed, the course meets 54 months, and the internship was onsite at the same institution. After that you clear FMGE and complete the 12-month CRMI in India. Verify the college on both lists before admission, not after.

What is the 7.5 per cent CRMI seat cap?

Older Indian medical colleges may allocate up to 7.5 per cent of intern seats to foreign medical graduates. New colleges without their own interns can offer more. In practice this creates waiting periods, which is another reason to clear FMGE early.

Can I do my internship in India instead of the Philippines?

No. The 12-month internship must be completed at the same foreign institution where you studied. The 12-month CRMI in India comes after that, so it is a second internship, not a replacement.

What if my college is not on WDOMS?

The degree will not support an Indian registration. WDOMS is the first filter NMC uses, and the 2026 notice makes State Medical Councils verify against it. Check before you pay fees.

Do I need NEET before joining BSBio?

BSBio is a pre-medical course rather than the medical degree, so the NEET requirement attaches to the MD admission that follows. Confirm the current position with NMC and the college before you pay for either. [The BSBio route explained](https://drdreams.in/without-neet.md).

Will NExT replace FMGE?

NExT is intended to replace FMGE, and the timeline has been deferred more than once. FMGE remains the active test, so prepare for the syllabus rather than the name. [A study plan by year](https://drdreams.in/fmge-next.md).

What is the 10-year limit?

The course and internship must be completed within 10 years of joining the foreign institution, including gaps and repeated years. The December 2023 notice states that graduates who exceed it lose eligibility for registration in India.

Do these rules apply to students who started in 2026?

If you enrol now, you are firmly under FMGL 2021, CRMI 2021 and the 2026 clarifications. That means 54 months, onsite internship at the same institution, NEET before the MD, WDOMS listing, and a 12-month internship in India afterwards.

Where can I ask about my own case?

Send the dates and the documents you have on the [contact page](https://drdreams.in/contact.md). DrDreams is not a regulator and cannot give you a ruling, but can tell you which paragraph of the notice applies and what the college should be putting in writing.

## Read the notice itself

The PDF is linked at the top of this page. If a college tells you something that contradicts it, ask them to put it in writing and check the date on their document.

[The main guide](https://drdreams.in/mbbs-in-philippines.md)

After the MD

# FMGE and NExT for Philippines graduates

You can do everything right for five and a half years and still not practise in India, because of one exam and one internship. Both are manageable. Both are usually planned too late.

Reviewed November 2026. These notes are written from having sat it, not from a coaching brochure. Rules change, so check NMC and NBEMS before you rely on anything here.

## FMGE, in short

Conducted by

NBEMS

Frequency

Twice a year

Format

Computer based, multiple choice

Pass mark

50 per cent

After passing

12 month internship in India

Then

State medical council registration

The part people skip

Clearing FMGE does not make you a registered doctor in India. You still complete a twelve month compulsory rotating internship here, and the 2026 NMC notice added detail on how that internship is verified.

Plan for roughly six and a half years from the day you land in Manila to the day you can register, and more if you need a second attempt.

The exams

## FMGE and NExT, without the panic

FMGE is a screening test for foreign medical graduates. It covers the Indian MBBS syllabus, which overlaps with what you learn in the Philippines but is not the same course. The differences are what catch people: Indian public health and forensic medicine content, and the Indian legal and ethical framing of clinical questions.

NExT is intended to replace it, as a common final-year examination for Indian and foreign graduates. The timeline for that has moved more than once, so do not build a plan around a date you read on a coaching website. Check the [NMC](https://www.nmc.org.in) notice, and the [rules page here](https://drdreams.in/mci-rules.md), which tracks the 2026 position with the official PDF.

Whatever the exam is called, the skills it tests are the same. That is why the plan below does not depend on which one you sit.

## Why first year, not final year

Medicine, surgery, obstetrics and gynaecology, paediatrics and community medicine carry most of the marks. In a Philippine curriculum you meet several of them properly in year three and four. If you start preparing in the final year, you are revising subjects you last opened two years ago, in the same months you are doing your internship and applying for the exam.

Starting early does not mean studying twelve hours a day from day one. It means keeping one Indian resource alive alongside your course, so that when the serious phase starts you are revising instead of learning.

The plan

## Five years, in slices

1.

### Year one: one subject, one hour

Pick anatomy and physiology. Watch Indian lectures for the topics your college is covering that week. You are not preparing for an exam yet, you are learning the Indian vocabulary for the same facts.

2.

### Year two: add pathology and pharmacology

Two to three hours a week, no more. Start a question bank and do ten questions a week. Keep a notebook of the ones you get wrong. That notebook becomes your revision list later.

3.

### Year three: clinical subjects begin

Now the ward and the exam start pointing the same direction. When you see a case, read the Indian guideline for it that evening. This is the year the two curricula stop feeling like separate courses.

4.

### Year four: full question banks and past papers

Weekly tests, timed. Ten years of past papers, at least. Join or form a group of three or four and teach each other, because teaching is the only way to find out what you do not actually know.

5.

### Internship year: revision and mock exams

Six to eight hours a day in the months before the exam, with mock tests on the same schedule as the real one. This is when the notebook from year two earns its keep.

Resources people actually use

Marrow, PrepLadder and DAMS are the three Indian platforms most students we have spoken to have used, and past papers from NBEMS. DrDreams is not affiliated with any of them and is not saying one is better. What matters is picking one and finishing it, not collecting three.

What works

## Habits that clear it

- **One resource, finished.** Students who fail usually have four subscriptions and no completed course.

- **Questions from the start.** Reading without testing yourself feels productive and is not.

- **A study group of three or four.** Not ten. Ten becomes a social club.

- **Timed mocks, on the real schedule.** The exam is a stamina test as much as a knowledge test.

- **Clinical work taken seriously.** The students who examine well and examine badly struggle on the clinical parts. Do both.

What fails

## Habits that sink people

- **"I will start after graduation."** By then you have forgotten the basic sciences you need most.

- **Only watching videos.** Video feels like studying. Recall is studying.

- **Ignoring community medicine.** It is a large, boring, high-scoring block that students skip.

- **Studying alone for two years.** Isolation is a bigger risk than a noisy group.

- **Planning around NExT rumours.** Study the syllabus. The exam's name will take care of itself.

Coaching

## Which colleges include it

Five of the six colleges covered here run FMGE coaching on campus: Gullas, Perpetual, DMSF, Brokenshire and Jose Maria, with the last two being smaller programmes. [Southwestern](https://drdreams.in/colleges/southwestern.md), where I studied, does not, which is why an online course was bought in second year.

On-campus coaching is worth more than it sounds, because it solves the discipline problem rather than the content problem. If your college does not have it, budget for a course and treat the subscription as a fixed monthly cost, the same way you treat rent.

[Compare the six on coaching](https://drdreams.in/colleges.md)

Questions

## What graduates ask

Is FMGE difficult for Philippines graduates?

It is difficult for everyone. Most candidates do not clear it on the first attempt, and the ones who do usually started preparing in the early years rather than after graduation. The exam tests the Indian MBBS syllabus, which overlaps with yours but is not identical.

Has NExT replaced FMGE yet?

NExT is intended to replace FMGE, and the timeline has moved more than once. Do not plan around a date you read on a coaching site. Check the current NMC notice, and the [rules page here](https://drdreams.in/mci-rules.md), before you make decisions based on it.

What happens after I clear FMGE?

You complete a twelve month compulsory rotating internship in India, then register with the state medical council. The internship is a requirement, not a formality, and the 2026 NMC notice added detail on how it is verified.

## Check the source

The rules on internship, the exam and registration are set by NMC and NBEMS, not by this site. Both are linked on the rules page, with the 2026 notice as a PDF.

[NMC rules 2026](https://drdreams.in/mci-rules.md)

Recognition

# Is MBBS in the Philippines valid in India?

Yes, but only if the college is on the NMC list, you pass FMGE or NExT, and you finish the Indian internship. Here is what each of those actually requires.

Last reviewed November 2026.

## On this page

1. The short answer

2. What "valid" actually means

3. Check one: the NMC list

4. Check two: WDOMS

5. The 2026 NMC rules

6. FMGE or NExT

7. The twelve month internship in India

8. Registration

9. The Philippine licence, separately

10. Why degrees fail at the last step

11. A checklist before you pay

## The short answer

An MD from a Philippine medical college is valid in India if three things are true: the college was on the National Medical Commission's list when you enrolled and when you graduated, you pass FMGE or NExT, and you complete a twelve month internship in India. Miss any one of those and the degree will not get you registered to practise.

"Valid" is not a property of the country. It is a property of the college, the year you joined, and what you do after you graduate. Two students can hold the same degree from the same university and have very different outcomes because one checked the list and the other trusted a brochure.

This page is the long version of that answer. The [NMC rules page](https://drdreams.in/mci-rules.md) has the official notice and the exact clauses.

## What "valid" actually means

People use "recognised" to mean three separate things, and that is where the confusion starts.

- **Recognition.** The college appears on the NMC's list of foreign medical institutions. This is about the college, not you.

- **Equivalence.** NMC treats the Philippine Doctor of Medicine as equivalent to the Indian MBBS for registration. This is about the degree.

- **Registration.** You pass the screening exam, finish the Indian internship, and your state medical council enters you in the register. This is about you.

All three have to line up. A college on the list does not register you. A passed exam does not fix a college that was never listed. And a degree from a listed college does not practise for you while you skip the internship.

## Check one: the college on the NMC list

Go to [nmc.org.in](https://www.nmc.org.in) and find the list of recognised foreign medical institutions. Search the college by its official name, not the short name in a WhatsApp forward. Names differ: a college may be listed under its university, its trust, or an older name.

Then check the same college on the World Directory of Medical Schools at [search.wdoms.org](https://search.wdoms.org). NMC's 2026 notice leans on WDOMS for verification, and a college that is absent there is a problem even if a consultant says otherwise.

Two practical notes. First, the list changes. A college can be added or removed, and the rules put the burden on the student to confirm status at enrolment and at graduation. Second, a screenshot is not proof. Take your own screenshot with the date visible, and ask the college for a written statement that it is listed for the year you are joining.

## Check two: WDOMS

WDOMS is not an approval body. It is a directory, run by the World Federation for Medical Education and FAIMER. Being in it does not by itself make a degree valid in India, and being absent from it is a red flag that NMC now treats seriously.

Use it for the details that brochures blur: the exact degree awarded, the address, the year the programme started, and whether the school is listed as a medical school or only as a health science institution. If the WDOMS entry and the brochure disagree about the degree name, ask the college to explain in writing.

## The 2026 NMC rules

The NMC public notice of 5 March 2026 tightened the route for foreign graduates. The parts that matter before you join:

- **The course must run at least 54 months.** A shorter programme, or one that compresses teaching into fewer months, creates a registration problem later.

- **The internship must be at the same university.** The twelve month internship has to be done at the institution that awarded the degree, not at a separate hospital arranged at the end.

- **Online teaching must be compensated.** If part of your course was delivered online, the college has to make up the lost time. Do not enrol in a programme that plans to teach a large share of the pre-clinical years remotely.

- **The whole programme must be completed within ten years.** Breaks, repeated years and deferred internships count against that window.

- **FMGL 2021 applies to students who enrolled on or after 18 November 2021.** If you joined after that date, the 2021 regulations govern you, not the older framework.

These are the rules as published. They can be amended, and state medical councils sometimes read them differently. Read the [full notice page](https://drdreams.in/mci-rules.md) and keep the PDF. If a consultant tells you a rule does not apply to your college, ask them to show you the clause.

## FMGE or NExT

After the MD you sit the Foreign Medical Graduate Examination, or its successor, the National Exit Test. FMGE is conducted by the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences. NExT is being introduced and is expected to replace FMGE over time. Until the transition is complete, check the current NBEMS information bulletin for which exam applies to your batch, the dates, the eligibility rules and the attempt rules.

The exam is not a formality. It tests the Indian clinical and pre-clinical syllabus, and the pass rate for foreign graduates has historically been low. The students who clear it usually started preparing in first year, not after the internship. The [FMGE and NExT page](https://drdreams.in/fmge-next.md) has a year-by-year plan.

## The twelve month internship in India

Passing the exam is not the end. You then complete a twelve month compulsory rotating internship, usually called CRMI, at an approved institution in India. The internship is supervised, rotating through the major departments, and it is the point where Indian hospitals see whether your clinical training was real.

Plan the internship early. Seats are limited, the application windows are fixed, and a gap between passing the exam and starting the internship costs you months. Ask your state medical council and the institution you are targeting for the current process, not a forum post from three years ago.

## Registration

With the exam passed and the internship complete, you apply to the state medical council where you intend to practise. Registration is what makes you a doctor in India. It is separate from the college's degree, separate from NMC's list, and separate from the exam.

Keep every document from the Philippines: the degree, the transcript, the internship certificate, the migration certificate, and the NMC and WDOMS screenshots from the year you joined. Registration offices ask for paper, sometimes years later, and a college that has changed its administration may be slow to reissue it.

## The Philippine licence, separately

India's registration is one thing. The Philippine licence is another, and it is now open too. Since November 2026 the Philippine Professional Regulation Commission lets Indian graduates of recognised Philippine medical schools sit the Physician Licensure Examination and register to practise in the Philippines. The Embassy of India, Manila confirmed it.

It does not change the Indian route. Whatever licence you hold in the Philippines, you still sit FMGE or NExT and complete the twelve month internship in India to practise here. [How the Philippine licence works](https://drdreams.in/ple-philippines.md).

## Why degrees fail at the last step

Most failures are not mysterious. They are one of these:

- **The college was not on the list when you joined.** A promise that it "will be listed" is not a listing.

- **The course was shorter than 54 months.** A fast-track programme creates a registration problem that cannot be fixed after the fact.

- **The internship was somewhere else.** The 2026 notice requires it at the same university.

- **Too much of the course was online.** The lost time has to be compensated, and a college that does not do it leaves you short.

- **The ten year window ran out.** Repeated years and long breaks are not free.

- **The exam was left too late.** FMGE is hard, and a failed attempt in the final year is a very expensive way to learn that.

- **The paperwork was incomplete.** Missing transcripts and internship certificates delay registration for months.

## A checklist before you pay

| Check | Where | What to keep |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The college is on the NMC list | nmc.org.in | Dated screenshot and a written statement from the college |
| The college is on WDOMS | search.wdoms.org | Dated screenshot of the entry |
| The course is at least 54 months | College curriculum | The current curriculum, in writing |
| The internship is at the same university | College | A line in the offer letter |
| The fee sheet is current | College admissions office | The sheet with the intake year printed on it |
| The refund rule is clear | College | What comes back if the visa is refused |

Six checks, in order, before any deposit.

If any of those cannot be produced in writing, stop. The [document checklist](https://drdreams.in/documents-required.md) and the [admission process](https://drdreams.in/admission-process.md) cover the next stage.

Questions

## Validity questions students ask

Is an MD from the Philippines equal to MBBS in India?

NMC treats the Philippine Doctor of Medicine as equivalent to MBBS for Indian registration, provided the college is listed and you complete the exam and internship. The degree itself is called MD, not MBBS. Do not let the name difference worry you, and do not let a broker use it to charge more.

Can I practise in India without clearing FMGE?

No. Registration requires the screening exam, and the twelve month Indian internship. There is no route around it for a foreign degree.

What if the college is removed from the NMC list after I join?

That is the risk the rules place on the student. The college being listed when you enrol is not a guarantee that it stays listed. Check the list again before you graduate, keep dated screenshots, and ask NMC directly if the status changes. This is one reason to prefer colleges with a long, stable listing.

Does the twelve month internship have to be in India?

For Indian registration, yes. The Philippine internship is part of your MD. The Indian CRMI is a separate requirement after you pass FMGE or NExT.

How many attempts does FMGE allow?

Check the current NBEMS information bulletin. Attempt rules and eligibility have changed before, and a number remembered from an old forum post is not a safe basis for a five year plan.

Is online teaching from the Philippines accepted?

The 2026 notice requires any online teaching to be compensated with equivalent on-campus time. A programme that plans to teach a large share of the course online is a risk, not a shortcut.

source: https://drdreams.in/after-mbbs-in-philippines.html

---

After graduation

# After MBBS in the Philippines: what comes next

The degree is the middle of the story, not the end. Here is the order from graduation to registration, and the realistic timeline for each step.

Last reviewed November 2026.

## On this page

1. The order of events

2. Come home and sit FMGE or NExT

3. The twelve month Indian internship

4. Register with a state medical council

5. PG in India

6. Jobs after registration

7. Options abroad

8. If you do not clear the exam

9. A realistic timeline

## The order of events

Graduation is not the finish line. The route from a Philippine MD to an Indian white coat has four gates, and they happen in a fixed order:

1. Graduate with the MD from an NMC-listed college.

2. Pass FMGE or NExT.

3. Complete a twelve month compulsory rotating internship in India.

4. Register with a state medical council.

You cannot swap the order. You cannot do the Indian internship before the exam. You cannot register before the internship. And none of it fixes a college that was not listed when you joined. If you have not checked that yet, read [is the degree valid in India](https://drdreams.in/is-mbbs-in-philippines-valid-in-india.md) first.

## Come home and sit FMGE or NExT

FMGE is the Foreign Medical Graduate Examination, conducted by the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences. NExT, the National Exit Test, is being introduced and is expected to replace FMGE over time. Your batch will sit whichever exam applies when you graduate, so check the current NBEMS bulletin rather than an old blog post.

The exam covers the Indian MBBS syllabus: pre-clinical subjects, para-clinical subjects, and the clinical subjects. It tests whether you can think like an Indian intern. It does not test how hospitals in the Philippines run, which is why students who only study for their college exams struggle.

The practical preparation starts in first year. Keep Indian subject notes alongside your Philippine lectures. Use FMGE question banks slowly, not as a last-year cram. The [FMGE and NExT page](https://drdreams.in/fmge-next.md) has a year-by-year plan and the mistakes that cost people a year.

## The twelve month Indian internship

After passing the exam, you complete a twelve month compulsory rotating internship, usually called CRMI, at an approved institution in India. It rotates through medicine, surgery, obstetrics and gynaecology, paediatrics, community medicine and the allied departments.

Indian hospitals use this year to see whether your clinical training was hands-on. Students who spent five years watching from a corridor feel the difference in the first month. Students who clerked, presented and assisted in the Philippines settle in faster.

Apply early. Seats are limited, states have different processes, and the window between passing the exam and starting the internship can be months. Ask the institution and your state medical council for the current process in writing.

## Register with a state medical council

With the exam passed and the internship complete, you apply for registration with the state medical council where you intend to practise. Registration is the legal step that makes you a doctor in India. It is separate from the degree, the NMC list and the exam.

Keep the paper trail: degree, transcript, internship certificate, migration certificate, exam pass certificate, and the NMC and WDOMS screenshots from your enrolment year. Registration offices can ask for documents years later, and a college that has changed administration may be slow to reissue them.

## PG in India

If you want an MD or MS in India, the route is NEET-PG. Foreign graduates usually need to clear FMGE or NExT and complete the Indian internship before they are eligible, but the eligibility rules are set in the current NEET-PG information bulletin. Read it for your year, not a summary from a coaching centre.

PG preparation is a different exam from FMGE. FMGE tests the undergraduate syllabus; NEET-PG tests applied clinical decisions in more detail. Most students take a year or two of internship and preparation before sitting it. Starting early is an advantage, but burning out in first year is not.

## Jobs after registration

Once registered, the ordinary options are:

- **Hospital medical officer.** Private and charitable hospitals hire registered doctors for ward duty, emergency and outpatient work.

- **Primary care and clinics.** General practice, family clinics and community health centres.

- **Government health schemes.** State health departments and national programmes hire medical officers on contract and permanent roles.

- **Corporate and insurance medicine.** Medical officers for companies, hospitals and health insurers, including claims and hospital review work.

- **Clinical research and medical writing.** A less clinical path that values a medical degree and clear writing.

- **Hospital administration and public health.** Usually after an additional degree or diploma.

None of these are guaranteed by the degree. They are the normal destinations for a registered Indian doctor, and the competition is the same as for any other graduate.

## Options abroad

A Philippine MD is also a starting point for licensing routes elsewhere. Each has its own exam, fees and eligibility rules, and each should be checked at the official source for your year.

- **United States:** USMLE steps and ECFMG certification. The college's WDOMS listing matters.

- **United Kingdom:** PLAB and GMC registration.

- **Australia:** AMC examinations and registration.

- **Canada:** MCC examinations and provincial licensing.

- **Philippines:** practising there has its own licensure route and residency rules. Check with the Philippine Regulatory Commission and the college.

These routes are expensive and slow, and they are not a fallback for a failed FMGE. Decide early if one of them is your plan, because the exam preparation starts years before graduation.

## If you do not clear the exam

It happens, and it is not the end of your medical career. The first step is to check the current attempt rules and eligibility window in the NBEMS bulletin, because they determine what you can do next. The second is to diagnose why you failed: not enough clinical exposure, weak pre-clinical foundations, exam technique, or simply starting too late.

Then build a plan with a date. A repeat attempt with a fixed schedule, question bank targets and weekly tests is very different from "I will study harder". If you are working while preparing, protect two uninterrupted hours a day and one long test every week. The students who clear on a second attempt usually change the method, not just the hours.

## A realistic timeline

| Stage | Typical time | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Graduate and collect documents | 1 to 3 months | Degree, transcript, internship certificate, migration certificate |
| Prepare and sit FMGE or NExT | 6 to 12 months | Indian syllabus, question banks, weekly tests |
| Apply for the Indian internship | 1 to 3 months | State council and institution applications |
| Complete CRMI | 12 months | Rotations, logbook, certificate |
| Register | 1 to 3 months | State medical council application |

From graduation to registration, with the waiting time included.

The whole sequence usually takes two to three years after graduation. Plan for it financially before you leave for the Philippines, not after you return.

Questions

## After graduation, in plain answers

Can I work in India right after the MD?

No. You need to pass FMGE or NExT, complete the twelve month Indian internship, and register with a state medical council. Only then can you practise.

Can I do PG in India after a Philippine MD?

Yes, through NEET-PG, usually after clearing FMGE or NExT and completing the Indian internship. The eligibility rules are in the current NEET-PG information bulletin.

What if I fail FMGE?

Check the current attempt rules, find out why you failed, and build a fixed study plan with a date. Many doctors clear on a later attempt. It costs time and money, not your career.

Do I have to do the internship in India?

Yes, for Indian registration. The Philippine internship is part of the MD. The Indian CRMI is a separate twelve month requirement after the exam.

Can I practise in the Philippines instead?

Yes, since November 2026. The Philippine Professional Regulation Commission now permits Indian graduates of recognised Philippine medical schools to sit the Physician Licensure Examination and register to practise in the country, which the Embassy of India in Manila confirmed. Before that, the reciprocity rule kept the route closed. The PLE licences you in the Philippines only. To practise in India you still sit FMGE or NExT and finish the twelve month internship. [The PLE, in detail](https://drdreams.in/ple-philippines.md).

Licensure

# The Philippine licensure exam, and what changed in November

For years the Philippine Physician Licensure Examination was shut to Indian graduates, because the law required India to give Filipino doctors the same right. In November 2026 the Philippine Professional Regulation Commission opened it. Here is what that means, and what it does not.

Reviewed November 2026. Based on the Embassy of India, Manila and the Philippine Professional Regulation Commission.

| Item | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Exam | Physician Licensure Examination (PLE) |
| Regulator | Professional Regulation Commission (PRC) |
| Who can sit it | Indian graduates of recognised Philippine medical schools |
| What it gives you | Registration to practise in the Philippines |
| What it does not | Registration in India (that is FMGE or NExT) |
| Confirmed by | Embassy of India, Manila |

The facts

## What changed

Philippine law lets a foreign medical graduate sit the PLE only if their own country gives Filipino doctors the same right to practise. India's position on that reciprocity was the block, and it kept the licence out of reach for Indian graduates.

In November 2026 the Philippine Professional Regulation Commission told the Embassy of India in Manila that Indian graduates of recognised Philippine medical schools can sit the PLE and obtain registration to practise medicine in the country. The Ambassador, Harsh Kumar Jain, announced it. The change also matters for India, because NMC's rules look at whether you have the right to practise in the country where you took the degree.

The record

## How the position moved, in order

Each step was a real document or decision, not a rumour. The June facts are in the Embassy's advisory on its own site.

1.

### CHED's letter, 8 May 2025

The Philippine Commission on Higher Education told the Embassy that the Doctor of Medicine meets the Foreign Medical Graduate Licentiate requirements: 54 months, the prescribed subjects, English, a twelve month internship, and a certificate of registrability.

2.

### House Resolution No. 73, 11 March 2026

The House of Representatives of the Philippines endorsed that the MD from CHED-recognised institutions complies with the NMC regulations for Indian students studying abroad.

3.

### Embassy advisory, 17 June 2026

The Embassy of India, Manila set out the position in writing, and noted that the reciprocity guidance was still awaited. This is the page to read on the Embassy's own site.

4.

### Embassy letter to the Philippine DFA, 8 October 2026

The Embassy asked the Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs for reciprocal recognition, pointing to the registration rights Filipino doctors hold in India.

5.

### PRC decision, November 2026

The Professional Regulation Commission confirmed that Indian graduates of recognised Philippine medical schools can sit the PLE and register to practise. This is the step that ends the wait.

The boundary

## What it does not do

Passing the PLE licences you in the Philippines. It does not register you in India. To practise in India you still sit FMGE or NExT and complete the twelve month Indian internship, whichever country licensed you first. The two are separate routes, and the PLE does not shorten the Indian one.

If your plan is to come home and work in India, nothing about this changes your timeline. The [FMGE and NExT page](https://drdreams.in/fmge-next.md) is the one you want. The PLE matters if you want the option to stay, work and be registered in the Philippines, or if you want your file to satisfy every NMC condition while you are there.

Before you rely on it

## What to check yourself

The rules are fresh, and a page like this one goes stale. Confirm the current position with the two authorities before you build a plan on it.

- The Professional Regulation Commission, at [prc.gov.ph](https://www.prc.gov.ph/), for the PLE schedule, the application requirements and the current eligibility rules.

- The Embassy of India, Manila, for the advisory text and any later update: [eoimanila.gov.in/edphilli](https://www.eoimanila.gov.in/edphilli).

- Your college's international office, for how its own graduates have applied and what it will put in writing.

This page states the position as reported in November 2026. If a newer notice changes it, write in and the page is corrected, with the date changed.

Questions

## Two questions, answered

### Can Indian graduates take the Philippine PLE now?

Yes, since November 2026. The Philippine Professional Regulation Commission permits Indian graduates of recognised Philippine medical schools to sit the Physician Licensure Examination and register to practise in the country. The Embassy of India in Manila confirmed the change. Before this, Philippine law required India to give Filipino doctors the same right, and it did not, so the route was closed.

### Does passing the PLE let me practise in India?

No. To practise in India you still sit FMGE or NExT and complete the twelve month Indian internship, whatever licence you hold in the Philippines. The PLE opens the Philippines route only.

Sources

## Where this comes from

- Advisory on Medical Education in the Philippines, Embassy of India, Manila, 17 June 2026: [eoimanila.gov.in](https://www.eoimanila.gov.in/advisory-on-medical-education-in-the-philippines).

- Education in the Philippines (Advisories for Indian Medical Students), Embassy of India, Manila: [eoimanila.gov.in/edphilli](https://www.eoimanila.gov.in/edphilli).

- Professional Regulation Commission, Philippines: [prc.gov.ph](https://www.prc.gov.ph/).

The November 2026 decision was confirmed by the Embassy of India, Manila and reported by the Indian press, including the Times of India and Medical Dialogues.

- [The NMC rules](https://drdreams.in/mci-rules.md): the March 2026 notice and the rules that decide your registration.

Choosing a city

# Cebu vs Manila vs Davao for MBBS

The city decides what your ordinary week feels like and what you spend outside tuition. Here is the honest comparison, including the parts the brochures leave out.

Last reviewed November 2026.

## On this page

1. The comparison table

2. Cebu

3. Manila

4. Davao

5. Cost of living

6. Indian food and community

7. Safety

8. Hospitals and clinical exposure

9. Weather and typhoons

10. Flights home

11. Which city suits which student

## The comparison table

The college matters more than the city. But the city decides what your ordinary Tuesday feels like, how much you spend outside tuition, and how easily you can get home. This table is the short version. The sections below are the detail.

| Factor | Cebu | Manila | Davao |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Colleges covered here | GCM Gullas, Southwestern | Perpetual Help (Las Piñas) | DMSF, Brokenshire, Jose Maria |
| Feel | Calmer second city, walkable pockets, island pace | Dense capital, fast, noisy, always open | Smaller southern city, relaxed, spread out |
| Rent and food | Moderate | Highest of the three | Lowest of the three |
| Indian community | Small but present | Largest | Smallest |
| Traffic | Manageable | The main daily tax | Manageable |
| Typhoon exposure | Exposed | Exposed, with flooding | Less exposed than the other two |
| Flights to India | One stop usually, sometimes direct | Most options, one stop or direct | Usually two stops |

Cebu, Manila and Davao for an Indian medical student.

## Cebu

Cebu is the second city of the Philippines and the one most Indian students picture when they imagine the country: an island, a busy port, a old Spanish core, and a lot of coastline within an hour of the college. It is smaller than Manila, cheaper, and easier to move around. Mactan airport sits on the island, so the trip home starts close.

Two of the six colleges covered here are in Cebu: [GCM Gullas](https://drdreams.in/colleges/gcm-gullas.md) in Banilad and [Southwestern University](https://drdreams.in/colleges/southwestern.md) in the city. The Indian batch at Gullas is large, and the one at Southwestern is smaller. That difference matters more than the postcode.

The trade is that Cebu is not Manila. There are fewer specialists, fewer big-public-hospital rotations, and a smaller Indian community. If you need a large diaspora to feel settled, Cebu will feel quiet. If you want the city to be the calm part of the decision, it is the easiest of the three.

## Manila

Metro Manila is not one city. It is sixteen, stitched together by highways that are never empty. The college covered here, [University of Perpetual Help](https://drdreams.in/colleges/perpetual.md), is in Las Piñas, south of the old city, which is quieter than the centre but still part of the same sprawl.

The advantage is scale. The largest Indian community of the three, the widest choice of Indian restaurants and grocery shops, the biggest hospitals, and the most flight connections. If you want a city that never makes you feel like the only Indian in the room, Manila is it.

The cost is time and money. Traffic eats an hour or two a day if you live far from campus. Rent is higher. The heat is heavier because the city holds it. And the flooding in the wet season is real, not a joke. Students who thrive here tend to live close to campus and treat the wider city as a weekend place.

## Davao

Davao is on Mindanao, in the south. It is cleaner and calmer than Manila, cheaper than both Manila and Cebu, and spread out enough that you will use transport daily. The three colleges here are [DMSF](https://drdreams.in/colleges/dmsf.md), [Brokenshire](https://drdreams.in/colleges/brokenshire.md) and [Jose Maria](https://drdreams.in/colleges/jmc.md).

DMSF has the strongest clinical reputation of the three, with a large patient load and a 3D anatomy lab. Brokenshire is smaller, with faculty who know your name and a smaller attached hospital. Jose Maria is the budget option, with medical missions and basic facilities. The spread inside one city is wider than the spread between cities.

The trade is distance. Davao is farther from India than Cebu or Manila, and most routes involve two stops. The Indian community is the smallest of the three, and Indian food is harder to find. If you are comfortable cooking and you want the lowest total cost, Davao is worth the trade. If you need frequent flights home, it is not.

## Cost of living

Tuition is set by the college. Living cost is set by the city and by whether you cook. The published 2026-2027 sheets put food and accommodation at 14,000 PHP a month at Gullas and 15,000 PHP a month at DMSF, Jose Maria and Brokenshire. Those are college estimates, not a market survey, and they assume shared accommodation and ordinary meals.

In practice, Manila runs higher than the other two for rent, transport and eating out. Cebu sits in the middle. Davao is the cheapest, but the gap is smaller than the tuition gap between colleges. Do not pick a city to save rent and then pick a college that costs two lakh more.

The bigger variable is food. A student who cooks rice, dal and vegetables most days spends a fraction of what a student spends eating out twice a day. The [cost page](https://drdreams.in/fees-and-cost.md) breaks this into lines you can actually budget.

## Indian food and community

Manila wins on food. Las Piñas and the wider metro have Indian restaurants, spice shops and grocery stores that stock atta, dal, ghee and pickles. Cebu has a smaller but real set of Indian restaurants and spice shops, concentrated in a few areas. Davao has the least; you will cook more, and you will learn to substitute.

The community matters for different reasons. A large Indian batch is company, shared notes, and someone to split rent with. It can also be a bubble that keeps you from learning the local language and making Filipino friends. A small batch is lonelier in the first month and usually forces you into the wider campus. Neither is better. Know which one you are.

## Safety

All three cities are ordinary places to be a student, and none is a war zone. The honest differences are about streets and hours. Manila has parts of the metro where you do not walk alone at night, and pickpocketing is a city problem. Cebu is calmer, with the usual advice about unlit streets and late nights. Davao has a reputation for strict local administration and feels orderly, though the usual precautions still apply.

The bigger safety issue for Indian students is not crime. It is health, heat, and the sea. Learn where the nearest hospital is, keep your embassy contact, save the college's emergency number, and do not swim at beaches with a red flag. The [student life page](https://drdreams.in/student-life.md) goes through the first month.

## Hospitals and clinical exposure

Manila has the largest hospitals and the widest case mix. Cebu has strong regional hospitals and a busy port population. Davao has DMSF's hospital network and Brokenshire's smaller attached hospital. For clinical years, the question is not the city's hospital count but which hospital your college attaches you to, how many students share each bed, and whether foreign students are allowed to examine patients.

Ask that question college by college. A big city with a big hospital is useless if your college sends forty students to one ward and lets them watch. A smaller hospital where you are allowed to clerk, present and assist is better training. The [college comparison](https://drdreams.in/colleges.md) includes hospital exposure for each of the six.

## Weather and typhoons

The Philippines has two seasons: hot and wet, and slightly less hot. The wet season runs roughly June to November, and typhoons are part of life. Manila floods in heavy rain, especially in low-lying districts. Cebu is exposed to storms that cross the Visayas. Davao is farther south and less exposed than the other two, though it still gets heavy rain.

Practical advice: keep a rain jacket, waterproof sandals, and a power bank. Keep copies of your documents in a waterproof bag. Follow PAGASA, the national weather service, rather than a group chat. And do not book a flight home in the middle of a typhoon without a buffer day.

## Flights home

Manila has the most connections to India, usually one stop through Singapore, Kuala Lumpur, Bangkok or the Gulf, and sometimes direct. Cebu is next, with one stop common and direct routes appearing and disappearing by season. Davao usually means two stops, often through Manila, which adds hours and a connection you can miss.

If you plan to go home every year, price the flights before you choose the city. A cheaper college in Davao can lose its advantage over five years if every trip home costs more and takes a day longer. If you plan to stay through the programme, this matters less.

## Which city suits which student

| If you are... | Start with | Because |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On a tight budget | Davao | Lowest living cost, and Jose Maria is the cheapest college of the six |
| Needing a big Indian community | Manila | Most Indian food, shops and students |
| Wanting a calmer city | Cebu | Smaller, cheaper and easier to move around than Manila |
| Planning to fly home every year | Manila or Cebu | Better connections, fewer stops |
| Wanting the strongest clinical volume | Davao (DMSF) | Large patient load and a dedicated anatomy lab |
| Wanting small classes | Davao (Brokenshire) | Smaller batches and more faculty attention |

Pick the city that matches the student, not the brochure.

The final decision is still the college, the fee sheet and the NMC listing. City is the third question, not the first. Read the [college comparison](https://drdreams.in/colleges.md) before you fall in love with a skyline.

Questions

## City questions students ask

Is Manila better than Cebu for Indian students?

Manila has the largest Indian community, the most food options and the best flight connections. Cebu is calmer, cheaper and easier to get around. Neither is better in general; it depends on whether you want scale or calm.

Is Davao safe for Indian students?

Davao is an ordinary student city with a reputation for strict local administration. The usual precautions apply: avoid unlit streets at night, keep your documents safe, and know the nearest hospital. It is not a conflict zone.

Where is the cheapest place to live?

Davao is the cheapest of the three for rent and food, followed by Cebu, then Manila. The difference is smaller than the difference between college fee sheets, so do not choose a city to save rent and ignore tuition.

Which city has the best hospitals for clinical training?

Manila has the largest hospitals, but what matters is the hospital your college attaches you to and how many students share each ward. Ask that college by college. A smaller hospital with real patient contact beats a large one where you only watch.

Do I need to speak Tagalog or Cebuano?

No. Medical teaching is in English and hospital charts are in English. Learning a few phrases in the local language helps with patients and daily life, but it is not required for the course.

title: "MBBS in the Philippines vs Russia, China, Georgia and Nepal"

source: https://drdreams.in/mbbs-in-philippines-vs-other-countries.html

Comparison

# MBBS in the Philippines vs other countries

The Philippines is the strongest English-medium, hands-on option in its price band. It is not the cheapest and not the closest. Here is the honest comparison.

Last reviewed November 2026.

## On this page

1. The comparison table

2. Language of teaching

3. Clinical access

4. Cost

5. Recognition and the exam at the end

6. Food, distance and daily life

7. Who should pick the Philippines

8. Who should pick somewhere else

## The comparison table

No country is "best". Each one trades something: language, cost, distance, clinical access, or the size of the Indian community. The table gives the common shape. The ranges are indicative, gathered from students and published brochures, not quotes. Verify every number with the college for your intake.

| Destination | Language | Commonly quoted total | Clinical access | The trade |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Philippines** | English | Rs 15 to 25 lakh | Hands-on in Philippine hospitals | Cost and distance; 5 to 6 hour flight |
| Nepal | English | Rs 40 lakh and above in many colleges | Similar to Indian teaching hospitals | Close to home, but seats and fees vary widely |
| Russia | Russian in the early years | Rs 20 to 35 lakh | Limited patient contact for foreign students in many colleges | Cold winters and a language year |
| China | Mandarin by the clinical years | Rs 20 to 30 lakh | Language barrier in hospitals | Food and language, despite strong hospitals |
| Georgia | English, with a heavy accent | Rs 25 to 40 lakh | Varies by college | Higher cost, cold winters, small Indian community |
| Kazakhstan | Russian and Kazakh | Rs 18 to 25 lakh | Varies by college | Fewer Indian students, less FMGE support |
| Uzbekistan | English in many newer programmes | Lower than the Philippines in many brochures | Varies by college | Newer route; check the NMC listing carefully |

Destinations Indian students commonly compare with the Philippines.

Two warnings before you use this table. First, a low headline fee often excludes hostel, food, flights and the extra year of language. Second, recognition is a property of the college, not the country. A listed college in Russia is a better bet than an unlisted one in the Philippines, and the reverse is also true. Check the college on the [NMC list](https://www.nmc.org.in) and [WDOMS](https://search.wdoms.org) before anything else.

## Language of teaching

This is the difference that changes the whole course. In the Philippines, lectures, textbooks, hospital charts and patients are in English. You start medical school on day one, not in a language class.

In Russia, China and Kazakhstan, the early years usually include the local language, and the clinical years may require it with patients. Some programmes teach in English, but the ward is still local. A student who cannot speak to a patient is not getting the same clinical training, however good the hospital.

Georgia and Uzbekistan often advertise English-medium programmes. The accent and the local language still matter in the hospital. Ask to speak to a current Indian student in the clinical years, not just the admissions officer.

## Clinical access

Philippine hospitals are busy, and foreign students are generally allowed to examine patients, take histories, assist in deliveries and stand in theatre. That access is the strongest argument for the country. It is also the thing brochures cannot prove. Ask a current student in the clinical years how many patients they clerked last month.

In several other destinations, foreign students watch rather than do. The rules vary by college and by hospital, and they can change. A country-level claim is not enough. Ask the college for its policy in writing, and ask a student who is already there.

## Cost

The Philippines usually sits in the middle: more than the cheapest Uzbekistan or Kazakhstan brochures, less than Georgia and many private Indian seats. The total for five and a half years, including hostel, food, flights and visa renewals, is commonly Rs 15 to 25 lakh. The [cost page](https://drdreams.in/fees-and-cost.md) breaks that into lines.

A cheap headline is not a cheap degree. Add the language year, the hostel, the food, the flights and the exam preparation. Then compare the total. A college that quotes four years is either describing an old programme or hiding a year.

## Recognition and the exam at the end

Every foreign route ends at the same place for an Indian student who wants to practise in India: FMGE or NExT, the twelve month Indian internship, and state registration. The country does not exempt you. The college's NMC listing is what makes the degree usable.

NMC's 2026 notice tightened the rules across all destinations: a course of at least 54 months, the internship at the same university, compensation for online teaching, and completion within ten years. These apply to the Philippines and to Russia, China, Georgia, Nepal and everywhere else. Read the [rules page](https://drdreams.in/mci-rules.md) before you compare fees.

## Food, distance and daily life

The Philippines is a 5 to 6 hour flight from India, with one stop common. Nepal is a short flight or a train and bus away. Russia, Georgia and Kazakhstan are long, cold and require a different wardrobe. China is closer than Europe but the food and language are a bigger adjustment.

Indian food is easiest in Nepal and Manila, present in Cebu and Davao, and harder in smaller Russian or Chinese cities. If you cook, the difference shrinks. If you do not, learn before you leave. The [student life page](https://drdreams.in/student-life.md) covers food, rent and the first month in the Philippines.

## Who should pick the Philippines

- **You want English clinical training.** You will speak to patients in English from the clinical years.

- **You want hands-on exposure.** Philippine hospitals generally let foreign students do more than watch.

- **Your budget is Rs 15 to 25 lakh.** That is the realistic range for the whole programme, not the first year.

- **You can handle distance and heat.** It is far from home, and the wet season is real.

- **You want a structured route with Indian seniors.** The six colleges here have Indian batches and, at four of them, FMGE coaching.

## Who should pick somewhere else

- **Your budget is below Rs 12 lakh all-in.** Look at the cheapest options carefully, and check the NMC listing twice. A cheap unlisted college is the most expensive mistake on this page.

- **You need to be close to home.** Nepal is the practical choice if a family emergency means a train rather than a flight.

- **You want a cold climate and a European degree.** Georgia or Russia may suit you better, at a higher cost and with a language trade.

- **You are not prepared to learn a language.** Then avoid Russia, China and Kazakhstan unless the programme is genuinely English-medium through the clinical years.

- **You want to practise in the country where you study.** The licensing route there is a separate decision, and the Philippines is not automatically the easiest.

The honest summary: the Philippines is the strongest English-medium, hands-on option in this price band. It is not the cheapest, and it is not close to home. If those two things are acceptable, it is a serious choice. If they are not, another country may fit better.

Questions

## Comparison questions students ask

Is the Philippines better than Russia for Indian students?

The Philippines teaches in English and generally gives foreign students more hands-on clinical work. Russia is colder, often cheaper in the first year, and usually requires Russian. Neither is universally better; it depends on language, budget and clinical access.

Is Nepal cheaper than the Philippines?

Some Nepali colleges quote lower fees, but the totals vary widely and many are not cheaper once hostel and other costs are added. Check the specific college's NMC listing and current fee sheet.

Is Georgia better than the Philippines?

Georgia is usually more expensive, colder, and has a smaller Indian community. It may suit students who want a European setting. The clinical access and language should be checked college by college.

Does the country affect FMGE?

No. FMGE or NExT applies to every foreign graduate, and the NMC rules on duration, internship and online teaching apply across destinations. The college's listing is what matters.

Which country has the cheapest total cost?

Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan often quote the lowest headline fees, but totals vary and the language and clinical access are trade-offs. Compare the whole programme, not the first-year number.
